title: All mine is with me
hook: Stilpo lost city, wife and children and said everything of his was still with him

segments.voice: Yesterday: an audience of one. Your line was one is enough. Did you do one piece of good work for one person, without counting who noticed? Day four hundred forty-three.

A city has just fallen. The conqueror, a king called Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger of Cities, rides through the smoke of Megara. His soldiers have taken what they wanted. Somewhere in the ruins stands an old philosopher named Stilpo, whose home is gone and whose wife and children are lost to him. The king, curious, asks him: have you lost anything? What Stilpo answered has been repeated for over two thousand years, and Seneca tells the story in his ninth letter. Today: all mine is with me.
screen: `MEGARA HAS FALLEN.` → `HAVE YOU LOST ANYTHING?` → `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. Stilpo told the king: I have all my goods with me. Seneca explains what he meant. Stilpo counted as truly his own only the things no one could carry off: his justice, his courage, his good sense, his character. The city, the house, even the people he loved most were real goods in the ordinary sense, but they had never been his to keep. Second, the hard part. It's fair to flinch at this story. Losing a family is not a small thing, and Seneca doesn't say it is. In the same letter he says the wise person feels their troubles, and then overcomes them. Not numb. Not untouched. Still standing. Third, the friendship twist. The surprising thing is where Seneca puts this story: in a letter about friendship. Lucilius has asked whether a person who is complete in themselves needs friends at all. Seneca says the wise person is content with themselves, and can live without friends if they must, but still wants them, very much. Not to have someone who'll sit at their bedside, but to have someone at whose bedside they can sit. Fourth, the balance. So Stilpo's line isn't a reason to love less. It's a reason to love without fear. If what's most yours can't be taken, you can give your heart to people and things freely, knowing that even if you lose them, you won't lose yourself. The Latin has stuck for centuries as a proverb: omnia mea mecum sunt. All mine is with me.
screen: `I HAVE ALL MY GOODS WITH ME.` · `FEELING IT, AND STILL STANDING.` · `WANTING FRIENDS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITHOUT FEAR.` · then, large: `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Take something to write on, or just count on your fingers. List a few things that are yours in Stilpo's sense, things no fire, thief or bad day could take from you. Your honesty. Your patience, on good days. The way you keep a promise. What you've learned. The love you give, even if it isn't returned. Name three, slowly. Then hold your hands together in your lap, as if holding them, and breathe. All of this is with you, right now. The bell holds the time.
All mine is with me. Stilpo's answer after losing his city: what is truly his, his character and good sense, could not be taken. Seneca's ninth letter. Today's word.
screen: `ALL MINE IS WITH ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all mine is with me. Keep your short list with you today. When something goes missing, a plan, a thing, a chance, touch the list once. Day four hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism reflect on which of their goods are truly their own, character, judgment, kindness, so that losses elsewhere do not take away their footing.

fork.setup: you're Stilpo, standing in your ruined city. the conquering king asks: have you lost anything? what do you say?
options: I have all my goods with me.
fork.reveal: he said everything that was truly his was still with him: not the city, but his justice, courage and good sense.

original.note: Latin: all mine is with me, Stilpo's answer as Seneca tells it.

trapdoor: what it means: Stilpo counted only his character as truly his, so losing his city could not take what was most his own.
what a scholar hears: Stilpo was a Megarian, not a Stoic, yet Zeno studied with him; Cicero tells a similar saying of Bias of Priene.

notes: Letter 9.18–19: Demetrius Poliorcetes takes Megara; Stilpo, having lost his children and wife, answers 'omnia mea mecum sunt'; Seneca glosses his goods as justice, virtue, temperance, prudence. Paraphrased; confirm the list of virtues.
Letter 9.3: the wise man 'feels' his troubles but overcomes them; 9.8: the wise man wants a friend in order to have someone by whose sickbed he can sit. Paraphrased; confirm.
Whether Stilpo's family were killed or captured is not specified by Seneca ('lost'); the script keeps 'lost to him'.
Zeno studying with Stilpo (Diogenes Laertius 7.2, 7.24) and Cicero's 'omnia mecum porto mea' attributed to Bias (Paradoxa Stoicorum 1.8): confirm.
